implementation_notes: SwiftData's metadata store is the macro annotation set on the model class: @Model makes the class persistable, @Attribute customises a property and originalName records its previous stored name, @Relationship(deleteRule:inverse:) declares links, @Transient excludes a property, and the macros expand into schema metadata held by a ModelContainer, with ModelContext and @Query as the engine surface for insert, fetch, update and delete. The class remains an ordinary Swift class, so the hand-written mapper disappears. When the mapping must be an explicit, versioned artifact, Core Data's model file or GRDB's declared table and columns are the alternatives.
pitfalls: Renaming a property without originalName (or a hash modifier) changes the store's model identity and breaks lightweight migration of existing data.
Macro-generated accessors change property semantics compared with a plain stored property, which affects observation and property observers.
Container-level schema problems - duplicate model types, malformed relationships - surface when the ModelContainer is created, that is, at application start.

variants.name: Core Data managed object model
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Apple stack keeps the mapping in an external, versioned model file: the .xcdatamodeld is compiled into an NSManagedObjectModel describing entities, attributes and relationships, and the entity classes declare @NSManaged properties that Core Data populates, with NSEntityDescription and mapping models handling versioning. The reader is the model loader and the engine is the managed object context, so mapping knowledge lives outside the code and can be migrated and versioned independently - the reason it survives in applications that must keep historical migrations working.
pitfalls: @NSManaged properties must match the model exactly: a mismatch crashes at runtime with 'unrecognized selector sent to instance'.
Model versions and mapping models are required for migrations, so editing the current model in place makes existing stores unreadable.
The model file is XML edited by Xcode, which diffs poorly and breaks under concurrent edits.

variants.name: GRDB records with Codable and explicit columns
variants.implementation_notes: GRDB's metadata is the Swift type system: Codable conformance together with CodingKeys or Column("...") constants and a static databaseTableName declare how properties map onto SQLite columns, and the record adapters are the reader and engine that bind statements and decode rows. Explicit Column enums keep SQL strings type-safe (the same constants are used in queries) while FetchableRecord and PersistableRecord provide CRUD from that one declaration, with associations and DatabaseValueConvertible for the rest. It suits applications that want explicit, testable SQLite access without Core Data's model files.
pitfalls: Codable maps by property name unless CodingKeys or Column constants pin the names, so a Swift rename silently changes which column is read.
Records are value types: identity and change tracking are explicit concerns (associations, observation), unlike Core Data's object graph.
